intro: How to plan, build and deliver presentations that actually work, using Microsoft PowerPoint. You will plan for an audience with a storyboard, design clear and accessible slides, use images legally, add charts, effects and links sensibly, then present with confidence and evaluate your work against success criteria.

pages.spec: Describe what presentation software is used for and explain why a presentation must suit its audience and purpose
pages.summary: Presentation software such as Microsoft PowerPoint shows information as a series of slides that support a speaker. Before you make a single slide, decide who your audience is and what your purpose is, because both change every design choice.

diagram.title: Who is it for?
diagram.caption: Match each audience to the design choice that suits it best.

Parents at a Year 8 information evening

blocks.text: You have probably sat through hundreds of presentations: in assembly, in class, maybe at a sports club awards night. Most of them used **[[Presentation software]]**: a program that shows information as a series of **slides**, one screen at a time. The best-known example is **Microsoft PowerPoint**, part of Microsoft 365, which you can use on the school network or online. Others include **Google Slides**, **Apple Keynote** and **Canva**.

A slide can hold text, pictures, charts, tables, sound and video. Slides are usually shown on a big screen or projector while someone speaks, but a presentation can also run on its own, for example on a touch screen in a museum or a TV in a school reception area.
What are presentations used for?

items: **To inform**: teaching a class about the water cycle, or telling parents about a school trip to Belfast.
**To persuade**: convincing the school council to put a water fountain in the canteen, or asking a local business to sponsor the rugby team.
**To entertain**: a quiz night, a photo slideshow of the Year 10 residential.
**To advertise or display**: a looping slideshow in reception showing this week's events, or a cinema showing adverts before the film.

blocks.text: Audience and purpose

Two questions come before everything else. Who is the **[[Audience]]** (the people who will watch it)? And what is the **[[Purpose]]** (what you want the presentation to achieve)? Get these right and the other decisions (how many words, which pictures, which colours, how long it lasts) become much easier.

head: Think about…
Questions to ask
rows: Will they understand technical words? Do young children need more pictures and fewer words?
Are they experts, or is this all new to them?
A small classroom, a big sports hall, or on their own on a screen?
Two minutes in assembly, or a full lesson?
Learn something, vote for something, buy something, or just enjoy it?
blocks.caption: Planning for your audience

blocks.title: Worked example: same topic, different audience
blocks.context: Orla is presenting about **Lough Erne** twice: once to a P3 class visiting the school, and once to her Year 9 geography class.
steps: **P3 class (age 7):** big photos of boats and swans, one or two words per slide, bright colours, a short video clip, about 5 minutes.
**Year 9 class:** a map, key facts (it has two parts, Upper and Lower Lough Erne), a chart of visitor numbers, key terms, about 8 to 10 minutes.
The topic is the same, but the audience changes the wording, the amount of text, the pictures and the length.
blocks.answer: The audience decides the design. One presentation does not suit everyone.

blocks.text: A very common mistake is to start by choosing a fancy theme and animations before you know who you are talking to. Decide **audience and purpose first**, design second.

Designers call this **analysing user needs**: finding out what the people who will use your work need from it, then designing around them. This is called **[[user-centred design|User-centred design]]**. The best way to find out is to **ask**: a quick survey or a chat with a few people from your audience beats guessing.
Formal or informal? Communication conventions

Every audience expects a certain style of communication. The accepted rules for how you communicate with a particular audience are called **[[communication conventions|Communication conventions]]** (sometimes called communication protocols). Choosing the right **tone** (how formal or informal you sound) is part of suiting your audience.

head: Formal
Informal
rows: Parents, a business, a judging panel, the school governors
Your friends, a class quiz, a club social
Calm theme, few effects, logo and contact details
"Good evening. Thank you for coming to our Year 8 information evening."
"Right, who's ready for the hardest quiz of the year?"

items: **A title slide** with the topic, your name and the date or event.
**An overview or agenda** for longer presentations, so the audience knows what is coming.
**A conclusion** that sums up the key points, and a slide inviting **questions**.
**A sources / credits slide** at the end, listing where your images and facts came from.
**No text-speak or emojis** in a formal presentation ("gr8", "u", 😂).

blocks.text: Being informal is not the same as being careless. Even a fun quiz for friends still needs correct spelling, readable text and credited images.

In CCEA's **Using ICT** framework for Key Stage 3, presentation work usually shows two of the five Es: **Exhibit** (presenting your work to an audience) and **Evaluate** (judging how well it worked and improving it). At GCSE you will be expected to explain how a product is designed to suit its **target audience**. The new Northern Ireland Digital Technology curriculum (TransformED) puts the same idea first: always ask **who** a design works for, not just whether it works.

head: Presentation
Written report
rows: Supports a speaker; key points only
Is read on its own; full detail

blocks.text: Write your audience and purpose at the top of your storyboard in one sentence, for example: *"To persuade the school council (pupils and two teachers) to fund a lunchtime coding club."* Check every slide against it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Presentation software shows information as a series of slides, e.g. Microsoft PowerPoint.
Presentations can inform, persuade, entertain or advertise.
The audience is who will watch it; the purpose is what it should achieve.
Audience and purpose decide the text, pictures, colours and length: this is user-centred design.
Follow the communication conventions your audience expects: formal or informal tone, title slide, conclusion, sources slide.
A presentation supports a speaker; it is not a report on a screen.

check.q: What is the **purpose** of a presentation?
o: The people who will watch it
What the presentation is meant to achieve
The theme and colours it uses
The number of slides it has
check.why: Purpose = what you want it to do (inform, persuade, entertain…). The people watching are the audience.

check.q: Which is an example of presentation software?
check.why: PowerPoint makes slide shows. Excel is a spreadsheet, Photoshop edits images and Access is a database.

check.q: A slideshow for P2 children visiting the school should have…
o: Big pictures and very few words
Small text so more fits on
check.why: Young children read slowly, so pictures and a few simple words suit them best.

check.q: Asking the school council to fund a new club is a presentation that aims to…
check.why: Trying to convince people to agree or act is persuading.

check.q: Which suits a **formal** presentation to parents at an information evening?
o: Slang and in-jokes to keep it lively
Polite full sentences when speaking and no text-speak
A different fancy font on every slide
check.why: A formal audience expects polite, clear language and a calm, professional style.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the **audience** and the **purpose** of a presentation.
practice.a: Audience: the people who will watch / use the presentation (1). Purpose: what the presentation is meant to achieve, e.g. to inform or persuade (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between a formal presentation to a local business and an informal quiz for your friends.
practice.a: Any two, e.g. formal uses polite language with no slang / text-speak, informal can be chatty (1); formal uses a calm professional theme and few effects, informal can be brighter (1); formal includes contact details / a clear request / sources slide (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways a presentation for a Primary 3 class should be different from one for a Year 10 class.
practice.a: Any two, e.g. fewer words / simpler language (1); larger, more colourful pictures (1); shorter overall (1); larger text (1); no technical terms (1).

pages.spec: Plan a presentation using a storyboard before building it
pages.summary: A storyboard is a plan of every slide, drawn before you open PowerPoint. It shows the content, layout, images, links and notes for each slide, so you can fix problems on paper instead of wasting time on screen.

diagram.title: From idea to finished presentation
diagram.caption: Click each stage. Planning comes before building, and testing can send you back to improve it.

nodes.label: Audience and purpose
nodes.detail: Who is it for, and what should it achieve? Write it in one sentence.

nodes.label: Research
nodes.detail: Collect facts, images and sources. Note where each one came from.

nodes.label: Storyboard
nodes.detail: Sketch every slide: layout, text, images, links, transitions and notes.

nodes.label: Build
nodes.detail: Create the slides in PowerPoint following the storyboard.

nodes.label: Test and rehearse
nodes.detail: Check links, spelling and accessibility; practise speaking with timings.

nodes.label: Present and evaluate
nodes.detail: Deliver it, collect feedback, and judge it against the success criteria.

blocks.text: Film-makers and game designers never start by filming or coding. They draw a plan first. For a presentation, that plan is called a **[[Storyboard]]**: a sketch of every slide, in order, with notes about what goes on it.

Making a presentation follows the same **development cycle** as making an app or a website: **plan, develop (build), test, refine**, and round again until it works well for its users. The storyboard is the planning stage.

Storyboarding can feel like extra work, but it saves time. It is much quicker to rub out a box on paper than to rebuild ten slides because you realised halfway through that your story is in the wrong order.
What goes on a storyboard?

head: Part of the plan
What to write or draw
rows: e.g. Slide 3: The Marble Arch Caves
Boxes showing where the title, text and pictures will go
The key points (not full sentences): remember, less is more
What picture, chart, video or sound, and **where it comes from**
The theme you will use on every slide
Which ones, and why (keep them simple)
Where each button or hyperlink goes, e.g. 'Next' to Slide 4
What you will say while this slide is showing
blocks.caption: What a good storyboard includes

blocks.title: Worked example: storyboarding one slide
blocks.context: Ciarán's presentation is *"Visit Fermanagh"* for a group of visiting pupils from a partner school in Spain. Here is his plan for slide 3.
steps: **Title:** Marble Arch Caves Global Geopark.
**Layout:** title at the top; a large photo of the caves on the left; three short bullet points on the right.
**Text:** Underground river and boat trip / Stalactites and stalagmites / About 20 minutes from Enniskillen.
**Image:** a photo from a free stock-image collection, credited in small text under the picture.
**Transition:** Fade (the same on every slide). **Animation:** none.
**Notes:** 'The caves were formed by water dissolving limestone over thousands of years…'
blocks.answer: A complete storyboard slide covers layout, text, images (with source), effects and speaker notes.

blocks.text: Linear or not?

Most presentations are **linear**: slide 1, then 2, then 3, in a fixed order. Some are **non-linear**: the user clicks buttons to jump to different slides, like a quiz or a menu. If yours is non-linear, your storyboard needs **arrows** showing where every button leads. You will learn how to build these on a later page.
Keep your storyboard beside you while you build. If you change your mind, update the storyboard too: your teacher may ask to see how your plan developed, and it is good evidence for an evaluation.
A storyboard is a **plan**, not a rough copy of the finished slides with every word written out. Use keywords and quick sketches. Neatness matters less than completeness.

items: Decide the **audience and purpose**.
List the main points: aim for one main idea per slide.
Put them in a sensible order: a title slide, an introduction, the main points, a conclusion, and a **sources / credits** slide at the end.
Sketch each slide and add notes.
Check the plan against your success criteria before you start building.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A storyboard is a plan of every slide, made before building.
It shows layout, text, images and their sources, colours, effects, links and notes.
Plan one main idea per slide.
Linear presentations go in a fixed order; non-linear ones use links to jump around.
Fixing a plan is quicker than rebuilding slides.

check.q: What is a storyboard?
o: A finished presentation printed on paper
A plan of every slide made before building
A list of the sources used
A slide that tells a story
check.why: A storyboard is a plan sketched before you build, so you can fix problems early.

check.q: Which of these does **not** need to go on a storyboard?
o: The file size of the finished presentation
check.why: File size is only known after you build it. The other three are part of good planning.

check.q: Why is it worth storyboarding first?
o: PowerPoint will not open without one
It makes the slides load faster
Mistakes are quicker to fix on paper
check.why: Changing a plan is quicker than rebuilding finished slides.

check.q: A presentation that always goes slide 1, 2, 3, 4 in order is…
check.why: Linear means a fixed order, one slide after another.

practice.q: State **three** things that should be included on a storyboard for each slide.
practice.a: Any three, e.g. layout sketch (1); title / text (1); images and their source (1); colours / fonts (1); transitions / animations (1); links / buttons (1); speaker notes (1).

practice.q: Explain **one** benefit of using a storyboard before creating a presentation.
practice.a: e.g. Problems with the order or content can be spotted early (1) so less time is wasted rebuilding slides (1). Or: everything needed (images, sources) is gathered in advance (1) so building is quicker (1).

blocks.text: Slide layouts and placeholders

When you add a slide (**Home > New Slide**), click the small arrow under the button to choose a **[[Slide layout]]**. A layout is a ready-made arrangement of boxes, such as *Title Slide*, *Title and Content*, *Two Content*, *Comparison*, *Section Header* or *Blank*. You can change an existing slide's layout with **Home > Layout**.

The dotted boxes on a layout are called **[[placeholders|Placeholder]]**. They say things like *Click to add title* or *Click to add text*. A content placeholder also shows small icons so you can insert a table, chart, SmartArt, picture or video straight into it.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing layouts
blocks.context: Aoibhinn needs: (a) a first slide with the presentation title and her name, (b) a slide comparing PS5 and Xbox, (c) a slide with a heading and bullet points.
steps: (a) **Title Slide**: a big title placeholder and a subtitle placeholder for her name.
(b) **Comparison** (or **Two Content**): two side-by-side boxes, each with its own heading.
(c) **Title and Content**: a title plus one content placeholder for bullet points.
blocks.answer: Title Slide, Comparison, and Title and Content.

blocks.text: Use placeholders instead of drawing your own text boxes for titles. PowerPoint and screen readers use the **title placeholder** to know what each slide is called, which helps with accessibility and with navigation.
Views

head: View
Best for
rows: Building and editing slides (the usual view)
Typing and reorganising all the text quickly
Seeing all slides as small tiles; reordering, hiding or duplicating slides
Seeing and printing each slide with its speaker notes
Watching the show inside the PowerPoint window
Presenting full screen: press **F5** to start from the beginning, **Shift + F5** from the current slide, **Esc** to stop
blocks.caption: PowerPoint views (View tab, or the buttons on the status bar)

blocks.text: Do not confuse **Slide Sorter** with the **thumbnails pane**. Both let you reorder slides, but Slide Sorter fills the whole screen with tiles and you cannot edit slide content in it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The ribbon holds tools in tabs and groups.
Thumbnails on the left; slide in the middle; notes underneath.
A slide layout is a ready-made arrangement of placeholders.
Placeholders are dotted boxes for titles, text and content.
Normal view to build, Slide Sorter to reorder, Slide Show (F5) to present.

check.q: What is a placeholder?
o: A dotted box on a layout ready for content
A slide that has been hidden
A picture used as a background
A note that the audience cannot see
check.why: Placeholders say things like 'Click to add title' and hold content.

check.q: Which view shows every slide as small tiles so you can reorder them easily?
check.why: Slide Sorter shows all slides as tiles for reordering.

check.q: Which key starts a slide show from the very first slide?
check.why: F5 starts from the beginning; Shift + F5 starts from the current slide.

check.q: On which ribbon tab would you find Pictures, Charts and SmartArt?
check.why: The Insert tab adds new objects to a slide.

check.q: Which slide layout is best for putting two things side by side with a heading over each?
check.why: Comparison gives two content boxes, each with its own heading.

practice.q: Name **two** parts of the PowerPoint window and describe what each is used for.
practice.a: e.g. Ribbon (1): holds the tools in tabs such as Home and Insert (1). Notes pane (1): where the speaker types notes the audience cannot see (1). Slide thumbnails pane (1): shows every slide so they can be selected/reordered (1). Status bar (1): shows slide number, views and zoom (1).

practice.q: Explain what a **slide layout** is.
practice.a: A ready-made arrangement / template for a slide (1) made of placeholders for the title, text and other content, e.g. Title and Content (1).

pages.spec: Apply good slide design: the 6x6 guideline, contrast, readable fonts, consistency, design themes and the Slide Master
pages.summary: Good slides are simple, readable and consistent: few words, strong contrast, clear fonts and the same style throughout. Design themes and the Slide Master let you set the look once so every slide matches.

diagram.title: Bad slide vs good slide
diagram.caption: The same information, designed two ways.

states.label: Hard to read
points: Yellow text on a white background
Every slide a different colour scheme

states.label: Easy to read
points: Dark text on a light background
One theme used on every slide

blocks.text: Your slides are there to **support** what you say, not to replace you. If the audience is busy reading a wall of text, they are not listening. Good design follows a few simple guidelines.
The 6x6 guideline

The **[[6x6 rule]]** is a guideline for text-heavy slides: **no more than six bullet points per slide, and no more than about six words per bullet point.** Use keywords and short phrases, and *say* the rest. It is a guideline, not a law: some slides need fewer words (a single photo and a title) and very few need more.

blocks.title: Worked example: applying the 6x6 rule
blocks.context: Rory's slide says: *"The Ulster Grand Prix is a motorcycle road race that has been held at the Dundrod circuit near Belfast and it is known as one of the fastest road races in the world, with riders reaching very high speeds on public roads that are closed for the event."*
steps: Pick out the key ideas: motorcycle road race, Dundrod circuit near Belfast, one of the fastest in the world, public roads closed for racing.
Turn each into a short bullet point of six words or fewer.
Move the extra detail into the speaker notes.
blocks.answer: Four bullet points: Motorcycle road race / Dundrod circuit, near Belfast / One of the world's fastest / Public roads closed for racing.

blocks.text: Contrast, colour and fonts

items: **[[Contrast]]**: the difference between the text colour and the background. Use dark text on a light background, or light text on a dark one. Avoid yellow on white, or red on green.

**Fonts**: choose a clear, plain font such as Calibri, Arial or Verdana (these are *sans-serif* fonts: no little 'feet' on the letters). Use one or two fonts at most. Avoid fancy script fonts for anything except perhaps a title.
**Size**: a common guideline is at least **24 point** for body text and around **36 point or more** for titles, so the back of the room can read it.
**Busy backgrounds**: a photo behind text makes it hard to read. If you must, add a solid shape behind the text.

blocks.text: Consistency: themes and the Slide Master

**Consistency** means every slide looks like it belongs to the same presentation: same fonts, same colours, titles in the same place, same transition. The easiest way is a **Design theme**: on the **Design** tab, click a theme to apply a matching set of colours, fonts and backgrounds to every slide at once. **Variants** (beside the themes) give different colour versions of the same theme.

Behind every theme is the **[[Slide Master]]** (**View > Slide Master**). It is the top slide in a hidden set of master layouts. Anything you put on the master, such as a school logo, a footer or a font change, appears on **every slide** that uses it. Click **Close Master View** to go back to your slides.

blocks.title: Worked example: putting the school logo on every slide
blocks.context: Erin's presentation has 15 slides and she wants the school crest in the bottom-right corner of all of them.
steps: **Slow way:** paste the crest onto 15 slides and try to line them all up exactly. If she moves it later, she has to move 15 copies.
**Better way:** **View > Slide Master**, click the top (largest) master slide, **Insert > Pictures**, place the crest in the corner, then **Close Master View**.
The crest now appears on every slide, in exactly the same place, and can be changed once.
blocks.answer: Use the Slide Master for anything that should appear on every slide.

blocks.text: In Microsoft 365, **Designer** (on the Design tab) can suggest professional layouts for the slide you are on. It is a useful starting point, but check that its choice still suits your audience and is readable.
Do not make every slide a different colour or font "to make it interesting". It looks messy and distracts from your message. Interest should come from your content and how you speak.

head: Do
Don't
rows: High contrast, a small set of colours
One or two plain fonts, 24 pt or more
Lots of fancy fonts, tiny text
A different style on each slide

blocks.title: Key points
items: 6x6 guideline: about six bullets, about six words each.
High contrast between text and background.
Clear fonts, large enough to read from the back.
Be consistent: one theme, same layout and transitions.
The Slide Master puts things like a logo on every slide at once.

check.q: What does the 6x6 guideline suggest?
o: Six slides with six pictures each
About six bullet points, about six words each
check.why: It limits text so the audience listens rather than reads.

check.q: Which colour combination has the best contrast?
o: Yellow text on a white background
Light grey text on a white background
Navy text on a pale cream background
Red text on a green background
check.why: Dark text on a light background is easy to read. Red on green is also a problem for many colour-blind people.

check.q: Erin wants her logo on all 20 slides in exactly the same place. What should she use?
check.why: Anything on the Slide Master appears on every slide that uses it.

check.q: Why should a presentation use one design theme throughout?
o: PowerPoint will not allow two themes
check.why: Consistency makes the presentation look like one piece of work and avoids distraction.

practice.q: Describe **three** features of a well-designed slide.
practice.a: Any three, e.g. limited text / keywords only (6x6) (1); high contrast between text and background (1); readable font size, e.g. 24 pt or more (1); clear, plain font (1); consistent theme/colours (1); relevant images (1).

practice.q: Explain how the **Slide Master** can save time when creating a presentation.
practice.a: Changes made once on the Slide Master, e.g. adding a logo or changing the font (1), are applied automatically to every slide, so they do not need to be done slide by slide / they stay consistent (1).

pages.spec: Explain copyright, ownership, intellectual property and licensing (including Creative Commons), credit sources correctly, and use AI-generated images honestly
pages.summary: Almost every image online is protected by copyright, so 'found on Google' does not mean 'free to use'. Use images you are allowed to use, such as your own, stock images or Creative Commons images, credit the source, and clearly label any AI-generated image.

blocks.text: It is tempting to type a search into Google Images, right-click, copy and paste. But most of those images belong to someone: a photographer, an artist, a company. They are protected by **[[Copyright]]**.
What is copyright?

Copyright is the legal right of a creator to control how their work is copied, shared and used. In the UK it comes from the **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**. You do not have to register anything or even add the © symbol: the moment someone takes a photo, writes a song or draws a picture, they own the copyright automatically. For most works it lasts for the creator's lifetime plus **70 years**.

Copyright is one kind of **[[intellectual property|Intellectual property]]** (IP): things people create with their minds, such as photos, music, writing, designs, logos, inventions and software. Just as you own your bike, a creator **owns** their work, even though it is not a physical object. Other kinds of IP include **trade marks** (protecting brand names and logos) and **patents** (protecting inventions).

A creator can give other people permission to use their work through a **[[licence|Licence]]**: a set of rules saying what you may and may not do with it. Breaking copyright is a **legal** problem (the owner could make you remove it or pay them); taking credit for someone else's work is also an **ethical** problem, because it is unfair to the person who made it.
"I found it on Google" is **not** permission. Google Images is a search engine: it shows you pictures from other people's websites. It does not own them and cannot give you permission to use them.
Using someone else's work and pretending it is yours is **[[Plagiarism]]**. In school that can mean losing marks; at GCSE and A level, coursework can be disqualified.
Where can I get images I am allowed to use?

items: **Your own** photos, drawings and screenshots of your own work.
**Stock images** inside PowerPoint: **Insert > Pictures > Stock Images**. With a Microsoft 365 licence (which the school provides), these can be used in your presentations.
**[[Creative Commons]]** images: creators choose to let others use their work for free, as long as you follow the licence conditions.
**Public domain** images: copyright has expired or been given up, so anyone can use them.

blocks.text: Creative Commons licences
Creative Commons (CC) licences are built from a few simple conditions. The most common:

head: Licence part
Short for
Means
rows: You must credit the creator. (Almost every CC licence includes this.)
If you change it, share your version under the same licence.
You cannot use it to make money.
You can share it, but you must not change it (no cropping or editing).
No rights reserved: use it freely, no credit required (but crediting is still polite).
blocks.caption: Creative Commons licence conditions

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a licence
blocks.context: Darragh finds a photo of Belfast City Hall on a photo-sharing site, licensed **CC BY-ND**. He wants to crop it and put it on his slide about Belfast.
steps: **BY**: he can use it if he credits the photographer.
**ND**: No Derivatives means he must not change it, and cropping is a change.
So he may use the **whole** photo with a credit, but he must not crop it. Or he could look for a CC BY image that allows changes.
blocks.answer: He can use it uncropped, with a credit, but cropping breaks the ND condition.

blocks.text: Crediting a source: attribution

**[[Attribution]]** means giving credit to the creator. A handy way to remember what to include is **TASL**: **T**itle, **A**uthor, **S**ource (where you found it, ideally a link) and **L**icence. Put a short credit under the image or on a **Sources** slide at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example: writing a credit
blocks.context: A photo called *Lower Lough Erne at dusk* by a photographer called *J. Maguire*, found on a photo-sharing website, licensed CC BY 2.0.
steps: Title: Lower Lough Erne at dusk
Author: J. Maguire
Source: the web address of the photo page
Licence: CC BY 2.0
blocks.answer: "Lower Lough Erne at dusk" by J. Maguire, from [web address], licensed under CC BY 2.0.

blocks.text: **Insert > Pictures > Online Pictures** searches the web with Bing and usually shows Creative Commons results only, but PowerPoint warns that **you** are still responsible for checking the licence. Click through to the original page to check it.

The same rules apply to music, video clips and text. Do not paste a song into your presentation, or copy paragraphs from a website, without checking you are allowed. If you quote a sentence, put it in quotation marks and say where it came from.
AI-generated images: use them honestly

**[[generative AI|Generative AI]]** tools can create a realistic picture from a typed description (a **prompt**), such as *"a heron standing on a jetty on Lough Erne at sunrise"*. Some versions of PowerPoint, and many websites, now include tools like this. They can be useful, but they raise new questions about honesty and ownership.

items: **Label it.** Anyone looking at a realistic AI image may think it is a real photo. Add a caption such as *"AI-generated image, made with [tool name]"* and list it on your Sources slide, with the prompt if your teacher asks for it.
**Never use it to mislead.** Do not present an AI image as a real photo of a real event, and never make fake images of real people (a **deepfake**). These can spread misinformation and hurt people.

**Ownership is not simple.** AI tools learn from huge collections of images made by real artists and photographers, often without asking them, and the law on who owns an AI image is still being argued about. Check the tool's terms and your school's rules.
**Follow age limits and school rules.** Many AI tools have minimum ages; use only the tools your school allows.
**Check it.** AI images often contain mistakes: extra fingers, nonsense writing on signs, buildings that do not exist.

blocks.title: Worked example: real or AI, and how to label it
blocks.context: Megan's slide about the Enniskillen Airshow uses an AI image of planes over Enniskillen Castle, because she could not find a free photo.
steps: Is it misleading? A viewer could think it is a photo of a real airshow, so it **must** be labelled.
Caption under the image: *"AI-generated illustration, not a real photograph. Made with [tool name]."*
On the Sources slide: the tool, the date and the prompt she used.
Better still, if a real photo matters for the point she is making, look for a Creative Commons photo of the real event.
blocks.answer: Label it clearly on the slide and on the Sources slide; never pass it off as a real photo.

blocks.text: Using AI to make an image and **not saying so** is dishonest, just like copying a photo and pretending you took it. In GCSE coursework, failing to declare AI use can lead to the work being disqualified.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Copyright is automatic: the creator owns their work (their intellectual property), whether or not it shows ©.
Found on Google does not mean free to use; a licence says what you may do.
Use your own images, stock images, Creative Commons or public domain images.
CC conditions: BY credit, SA share alike, NC no money, ND no changes; CC0 = no conditions.
Credit sources with TASL: Title, Author, Source, Licence.
Label AI-generated images clearly and never use them to mislead.

check.q: When does a photographer get copyright on a photo they take?
o: Only if it shows the © symbol
Automatically, as soon as it is taken
Only once it is published online
check.why: In the UK copyright is automatic; no registration or symbol is needed.

check.q: What does **NC** mean in a Creative Commons licence?
o: Non-Commercial: you cannot use it to make money
New Copy: you must share it again
check.why: NC = Non-Commercial. No Changes is ND (No Derivatives).

check.q: What does TASL stand for when crediting an image?
check.why: Title, Author, Source and Licence are what a good credit includes.

check.q: Pasting someone else's work and presenting it as your own is called…
check.why: Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work as your own; attribution is the opposite.

check.q: Ronan uses an AI tool to make a realistic picture of the Erne in flood for his slide. What should he do?
o: Say he took the photo himself
Label it as AI-generated and list the tool in his sources
Add a CC BY licence to it
Nothing, AI images never need a label
check.why: A realistic AI image could be mistaken for a real photo, so it must be clearly labelled.

practice.q: Explain why a pupil should not just copy any image from a Google Images search into their presentation.
practice.a: Most images are protected by copyright / belong to someone else (1); using them without permission could break the law / is not allowed, and Google does not own the images so cannot give permission (1).

practice.q: An image is licensed **CC BY-SA**. Explain what a pupil must do if they edit the image and use it.
practice.a: BY: credit / attribute the creator (1). SA: share their edited version under the same licence (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** reasons why AI-generated images in a presentation should be clearly labelled.
practice.a: Any two: they can look like real photos so viewers may be misled (1); it is honest / avoids passing off work as your own (1); schools / exam boards require AI use to be declared (1); the image may contain mistakes or not show a real place/event (1).

pages.spec: Use charts, tables and SmartArt to present information clearly
pages.summary: Numbers are easier to understand as a chart, comparisons fit neatly in a table, and SmartArt turns lists into diagrams such as processes, cycles and hierarchies. Pick the one that matches what the information shows.

diagram.title: Pick the best tool
diagram.caption: Match each piece of information to the best way to show it.
pairs: Goals scored by six players
Column chart
How pupils travel to school, as shares of the whole
Pie chart
Temperature in Enniskillen each day for a month
Line chart
Prices of three phones with four features each
Table
The stages of the water cycle
SmartArt cycle
Who reports to whom in the school's senior team
SmartArt hierarchy

blocks.text: A slide full of numbers is hard to follow. *"Fifty-two pupils walk, eighty-seven come by bus, thirty-one by car…"* Turning information into a **chart**, **table** or diagram lets the audience see the point in seconds.
Charts

A **Chart** shows numbers as a picture. Use **Insert > Chart** (or the chart icon in a content placeholder), choose the type, and a small spreadsheet window opens where you type or paste your data. The chart updates as you type. If your data is already in Excel, you can copy the chart from Excel and paste it into PowerPoint.

head: Chart type
Best for
Example
rows: Number of pupils in each house
Visitors to the Marble Arch Caves each month
Parts of a whole (adds up to 100%)
How Year 9 pupils travel to school
blocks.caption: Choosing a chart type

blocks.text: Give every chart a **title** and label the **axes** (or use data labels). A chart without labels is just coloured shapes.
Tables

A table (**Insert > Table**) suits information that needs to be compared across several headings, such as the prices and features of three tablets, or a timetable. Keep tables small on a slide: three or four columns and a handful of rows. If it does not fit at 24 point, it is too big for one slide.
SmartArt
**[[SmartArt]]** turns a list into a ready-designed diagram. Use **Insert > SmartArt**, or select a bulleted list and click **Home > Convert to SmartArt**. It comes in categories:

head: SmartArt type
Shows
Example
rows: Three reasons to join the coding club
How to make a cup of tea
The water cycle; plan, build, test, improve
Levels, like a family tree or chart of who is in charge
blocks.caption: Common SmartArt categories

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing the right visual
blocks.context: Seán has three pieces of information for his slides: (a) the number of pupils in each Year 8 class, (b) the five steps for logging on to the school network, (c) how the 120 Year 8 pupils voted for a trip destination (Belfast Zoo, W5, or the Ulster Folk Museum).
steps: (a) Comparing separate classes: **column chart**.
(b) Steps in a fixed order: **SmartArt process**.
(c) Shares of a whole group: **pie chart** (a column chart would also work).
blocks.answer: Column chart, SmartArt process, pie chart.

blocks.text: Do not use a **line** chart for separate categories (such as classes or houses). A line suggests the values change smoothly from one category to the next, which makes no sense for 8A, 8B and 8C.
3D charts may look exciting but they often make values harder to compare. A simple flat chart is usually clearer.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Charts turn numbers into pictures: column to compare, line for change over time, pie for parts of a whole.
Always add a title and labels to a chart.
Tables suit comparisons across several headings; keep them small.
SmartArt turns lists into diagrams: list, process, cycle, hierarchy, relationship.
Choose the visual that matches what the information shows.

check.q: Which chart is best for showing how something changes over time?
check.why: A line chart shows a trend over time.

check.q: Which SmartArt type would you use to show the steps for saving a file, in order?
check.why: A process diagram shows steps in sequence.

check.q: A pie chart is best used when…
o: The values are parts of one whole
Comparing two years side by side
check.why: Pie charts show shares of a whole, like percentages that add up to 100.

check.q: Which option converts a bulleted list straight into a diagram?
check.why: Convert to SmartArt on the Home tab turns a list into a SmartArt diagram.

practice.q: A pupil wants to show how the number of visitors to the Fermanagh Lakeland Forum changed each month over a year. Name the most suitable chart and give a reason.
practice.a: Line chart (1) because it shows change / trend over time (1).

practice.q: Explain why a chart can be better than a list of numbers on a slide.
practice.a: The audience can see patterns / comparisons quickly (1) without reading and remembering lots of numbers (1).

pages.spec: Use transitions and animations sensibly, choosing effects, order and timing to support the message
pages.summary: Transitions play between slides; animations make objects on a slide enter, move or leave. Used sparingly and consistently they guide attention; overused they distract and look unprofessional.

diagram.title: One slide, step by step
diagram.caption: How the animations on one slide play in order. Click each step.

items.label: Transition: Fade
items.detail: Slide 4 fades in from slide 3. The same subtle transition is used on every slide.

items.label: Click 1: Title appears
items.detail: Entrance effect (green star): Fade, On Click.

items.label: Click 2: First bullet point
items.detail: Entrance effect: Appear, so the audience only reads the point being talked about.

items.label: With Previous: photo appears
items.detail: Starts at the same time as the bullet point, so no extra click is needed.

items.label: Click 3: Key fact pulses
items.detail: Emphasis effect (yellow star): Pulse, drawing attention to the important number.

items.label: After Previous: summary box
items.detail: Starts automatically 1 second after the pulse finishes (Delay 01.00).

blocks.text: PowerPoint can make things spin, bounce, fly and explode. It is great fun to try, but an audience quickly gets tired of it. The rule is simple: **every effect should have a reason.**
Transitions

A **[[Transition]]** is the effect that plays when the show moves from one slide to the next, such as Fade, Push, Wipe or Morph. Find them on the **Transitions** tab. You can set the **Duration** (how long the effect takes), add a sound (usually best avoided), and choose **Apply To All** so every slide matches.
Under **Advance Slide** you can choose **On Mouse Click**, or tick **After** and enter a time so the slide moves on by itself, which is useful for a looping display in reception.

**Morph** (in Microsoft 365) is clever: duplicate a slide, move or resize an object on the copy, then apply Morph to the second slide. PowerPoint smoothly animates the change between the two. It looks professional with no fiddly settings.
Animations

An **[[Animation]]** is an effect on a single object on a slide: a title, a picture, a bullet point. Select the object, then choose an effect on the **Animations** tab. Click **Add Animation** to put a second effect on the same object. There are four groups:

head: Type
Star colour
What it does
Example
rows: Brings an object onto the slide
Bullet points appear one at a time
Draws attention to something already there
A key number pulses or grows
Removes an object from the slide
Moves an object along a route
A boat moves across a map of Lough Erne
blocks.caption: The four types of animation effect

blocks.text: Order and timing
Open the **Animation Pane** to see every animation on the slide in order. Drag to reorder. For each one, set:

items: **Start**: **On Click** (waits for a click), **With Previous** (plays at the same time as the one before) or **After Previous** (plays automatically when the one before finishes).
**Duration**: how long the effect takes, e.g. 00.50 seconds.
**Delay**: how long to wait before it starts.

blocks.title: Worked example: bullet points one at a time
blocks.context: Niamh has four bullet points and wants each one to appear when she is ready to talk about it, without any extra clicks for the matching pictures.
steps: Select the text placeholder and choose the **Appear** or **Fade** entrance effect. By default each bullet point gets its own **On Click**.
Select each picture, give it the same entrance effect and set **Start: With Previous**.
Open the **Animation Pane** and drag each picture to sit directly under its bullet point.
Press **Shift + F5** to test the slide.
blocks.answer: Four clicks: each shows one bullet point and its picture together.

blocks.text: Using effects sensibly

head: Sensible
Overdone
rows: One subtle transition on every slide
A different flashy transition on each slide
Reveal points one at a time; highlight a key fact
Every word bounces, spins or flies in
Slow effects that keep the audience waiting
None, or one with a clear reason
Whooshes and applause on every click

blocks.text: Too many effects make a presentation look childish, slow it down and pull attention away from **what you are saying**. If an effect does not help the audience understand, delete it.

Effects can also cause problems for some people: fast, flashing or spinning movement can be uncomfortable for people with vestibular conditions or photosensitive epilepsy. Another good reason to keep things calm.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Transitions play between slides; animations act on objects within a slide.
Animation types: entrance (green), emphasis (yellow), exit (red), motion path.
Start options: On Click, With Previous, After Previous; plus duration and delay.
Use the Animation Pane to see and reorder effects.
Every effect needs a reason: keep them subtle and consistent.

check.q: What is the difference between a transition and an animation?
o: A transition plays between slides; an animation acts on one object
A transition acts on one object; an animation plays between slides
Transitions add sound; animations add video
check.why: Transitions = between slides. Animations = objects on a slide.

check.q: Which type of animation brings an object onto the slide?
check.why: Entrance effects (green stars) bring objects in.

check.q: An animation set to **After Previous** will…
o: Play automatically when the previous one finishes
Play at exactly the same time as the previous one
Only play once the slide show ends
check.why: After Previous starts on its own after the one before has finished. With Previous starts at the same time.

check.q: Which is the most sensible use of animation in a class presentation?
o: A different sound on every click
Bullet points appearing one at a time
Each slide using a new transition
check.why: Revealing points one at a time keeps the audience with the speaker.

check.q: Where can you see all the animations on a slide in order and drag to reorder them?
check.why: The Animation Pane lists every effect on the slide in order.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **transition** and an **animation**.
practice.a: A transition is an effect that plays when moving from one slide to the next (1). An animation is an effect applied to an object on a slide, e.g. text or an image (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why a presenter should not use too many animations.
practice.a: Any two, e.g. distracts the audience from the message (1); looks unprofessional / childish (1); slows the presentation down / wastes time (1); can be uncomfortable for some viewers (1).

pages.spec: Create hyperlinks and action buttons to build non-linear presentations such as quizzes and kiosk displays
pages.summary: Hyperlinks and action buttons let the user jump to any slide, a website or a file. This makes non-linear presentations possible, such as a menu, a quiz with right and wrong answer slides, or a self-running kiosk.

diagram.title: A non-linear quiz
diagram.caption: Each answer button links to a different slide. Click each stage.

nodes.label: Menu
nodes.detail: Buttons: Start quiz, How to play, Credits. Each is a hyperlink to a slide.

nodes.label: Question 1
nodes.detail: Which county is Enniskillen in? Three answer buttons.

nodes.label: Correct!
nodes.detail: Fermanagh is right. A Next button links to Question 2.

nodes.label: Try again
nodes.detail: The wrong answers both link here. A Back button returns to Question 1.

nodes.label: Question 2
nodes.detail: And so on. A Home button on every slide returns to the menu.

blocks.text: A normal presentation is **linear**: it goes forward one slide at a time. A **[[Non-linear presentation]]** lets the user choose where to go next by clicking. Think of a museum touch screen, a 'choose your own adventure' story, or a quiz that shows a different slide for right and wrong answers.
Hyperlinks
A **[[Hyperlink]]** is clickable text or an object that jumps somewhere else. Select some text, a picture or a shape, then **Insert > Link** (or press **Ctrl + K**). You can link to:

items: **Place in This Document**: any slide in the same presentation, e.g. *Slide 5* or *Last Slide*.
**Existing File or Web Page**: a website address or another file.
**E-mail Address**: opens a new email.

blocks.text: Hyperlinks only work in **Slide Show** view. In Normal view you need to **Ctrl + click** them.
Action buttons

An **[[Action button]]** is a ready-made shape with an icon, such as Home, Back, Next, End or Information. Find them at the bottom of **Insert > Shapes > Action Buttons**. Draw one on the slide and the **Action Settings** box opens, where you choose **Hyperlink to:** Next Slide, Previous Slide, First Slide, Last Slide or a particular slide. You can also add an action to any shape or picture with **Insert > Action**, and choose whether it happens on **Mouse Click** or **Mouse Over**.

blocks.title: Worked example: wiring up a quiz question
blocks.context: Slide 3 asks: *Which county is Enniskillen in?* with three buttons: **Tyrone**, **Fermanagh**, **Armagh**. Slide 4 says *Correct!* and slide 5 says *Try again*.
steps: Select the **Fermanagh** button, **Insert > Link > Place in This Document**, choose **Slide 4**.
Link the **Tyrone** and **Armagh** buttons to **Slide 5**.
On slide 5, add a **Back** action button that links to **Slide 3** (not 'Previous Slide': see the warning below).
On slide 4, add a **Next** button linking to the next question.
Test every button in Slide Show view.
blocks.answer: Right answer to slide 4, both wrong answers to slide 5, and every slide has a way back.

blocks.text: **'Previous Slide' is not the same as 'Last Slide Viewed'.** Previous Slide always goes to the slide numbered one lower. If your 'Try again' slide is slide 7, Previous Slide goes to slide 6, which might be a different question. Link to the exact slide, or use **Last Slide Viewed**.
Kiosk mode

**[[Kiosk mode]]** turns a presentation into a self-running display, like the screen at a visitor centre. Go to **Slide Show > Set Up Slide Show** and choose **Browsed at a kiosk (full screen)**. In kiosk mode:

items: Clicking the mouse or pressing keys does **not** move to the next slide, so users can only use your buttons and links.
Slides can also move on using **timings** (Transitions > After).
The show **loops** back to the start until someone presses **Esc**.

blocks.text: **Insert > Zoom** (Microsoft 365) makes a menu slide automatically: **Summary Zoom** creates a slide of clickable thumbnails, and clicking one zooms into that part of the presentation and back again.
In a kiosk or quiz, every slide needs a way to move on or get back, such as a **Home** button. Otherwise users get stuck on a dead-end slide. Test every single link before you present.
The way a user moves around a set of linked slides or web pages is called **navigation**. Planning it on your storyboard with arrows is exactly what web designers do with a site map.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Non-linear presentations let users choose where to go by clicking.
Hyperlinks (Insert > Link, Ctrl + K) can go to a slide, a web page, a file or an email.
Action buttons are ready-made shapes such as Home, Back and Next.
Kiosk mode: clicks do not advance slides, and the show loops until Esc.
Every slide needs a way out; test every link in Slide Show view.

check.q: Which keyboard shortcut inserts a hyperlink?
check.why: Ctrl + K opens the Insert Link box.

check.q: A museum wants a screen where visitors click buttons to choose a topic. This is a…
check.why: Users choose their own route through the slides, so it is non-linear.

check.q: In kiosk mode, what happens when a user clicks on an empty part of the slide?
o: Nothing: it does not move to the next slide
It goes to the next slide
check.why: In kiosk mode clicks only work on links and buttons, not to advance.

check.q: Where are action buttons found?
check.why: Action buttons are at the bottom of the Insert > Shapes menu.

practice.q: Describe how hyperlinks could be used to create a quiz in PowerPoint.
practice.a: Each answer option is a button/text with a hyperlink (1); the correct answer links to a 'correct' slide (1); wrong answers link to a 'try again' slide with a link back to the question (1).

practice.q: State **two** features of a presentation set up to be **browsed at a kiosk**.
practice.a: Any two: runs full screen (1); clicking does not advance slides / user must use buttons or links (1); loops continuously until Esc is pressed (1); can advance with timings (1).

pages.spec: Apply accessibility guidelines and international standards (WCAG) to a presentation using alt text, contrast, colour-blind friendly colours, readable font sizes and the Accessibility Checker
pages.summary: An accessible presentation can be used by everyone, including people who are blind, partially sighted, colour blind or dyslexic. Follow the international WCAG guidelines: add alt text, never rely on colour alone, use large high-contrast text, and run Review > Check Accessibility.

diagram.title: Spot the accessibility problem
diagram.caption: What is the fix? Click a hidden cell to check.
head: Problem
Fix
rows: Add alt text describing its purpose
'Correct answers are in green, wrong in red'
Add a tick or cross, or a word, not colour alone
Plain sans-serif font, at least 24 pt
Increase the contrast, e.g. dark grey or black
Three slides all with no title
Give every slide a unique title
A video with speech but no captions

blocks.text: **[[Accessibility]]** means designing so that **everyone** can use your work, including people with a disability. In any class or audience there are likely to be people who are colour blind, dyslexic, partially sighted, or who use a **[[screen reader|Screen reader]]** (software that reads out what is on the screen). A few simple habits help them all, and usually make the presentation clearer for everyone else too.
Alt text

**[[Alt text]]** (alternative text) is a short written description of an image, chart or other visual. A screen reader reads it aloud, so someone who cannot see the picture still knows what it shows. Right-click the picture and choose **View Alt Text** (or **Edit Alt Text**, depending on your version). Microsoft 365 may suggest a description automatically: always check it, because it can be wrong.

blocks.title: Worked example: writing alt text
blocks.context: Slide: *Enniskillen Castle*. Image: a photo of the castle's Watergate with the river in front.
steps: Weak: *"image1.jpg"* (tells the listener nothing).
Weak: *"Picture"* (still nothing useful).
Too long: a whole paragraph about the stonework, sky and every tree.
Good: *"The Watergate of Enniskillen Castle, with two round towers, beside the River Erne."*
blocks.answer: Describe what the image shows and why it is there, in one or two short sentences.

blocks.text: If a picture is only decoration (a swirl or border), tick **Mark as decorative** in the Alt Text pane so a screen reader skips it.
Colour blindness

About **1 in 12 men** and **1 in 200 women** are colour blind. The most common type makes **red and green** hard to tell apart. In a class of 30, there is a good chance at least one person cannot see your colour-coding.

items: Never use **colour alone** to show meaning. Add a label, a symbol (✓ ✗) or a pattern.
Avoid red text on green, or green on red.
In charts, add **data labels** so values can be read without matching colours to a key.
Use strong contrast between text and background.

blocks.text: Text that everyone can read

items: **Large text**: at least 24 point for body text.
**Plain fonts**: sans-serif fonts such as Calibri, Arial or Verdana are easier for many people with dyslexia to read than script or decorative fonts.
**Avoid** long blocks of text, all CAPITALS, lots of italics and underlining for emphasis (underlined text looks like a link). Use **bold** instead.
**Left-align** text rather than fully justifying it, so the spaces between words stay even.
**A unique title on every slide**: screen reader users jump between slides by their titles.

blocks.text: The Accessibility Checker

PowerPoint can check for you. Go to **Review > Check Accessibility**. The **[[Accessibility Checker]]** lists **Errors** (things that make content very hard to use, like missing alt text), **Warnings** and **Tips**, such as slides with no title, hard-to-read contrast or a confusing **reading order**. Click each problem to jump to it and see how to fix it.
International standards: WCAG

Accessibility is not just good manners: designers have a **responsibility** to include everyone, and there are agreed rules for doing it. The best known are the **[[WCAG]]** (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines), an **international standard** written by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). They were written for websites and apps, but the same ideas apply to presentations, especially ones shared online. UK public sector websites, such as council and government sites, are expected to meet them.

head: WCAG principle
Means
In a presentation
rows: Everyone can see or hear the content somehow
Buttons big enough to click; nothing that flashes
Clear language, slide titles, consistent layout
Real titles and placeholders a screen reader can find
blocks.caption: The four WCAG principles (remember POUR)

blocks.title: Worked example: does the text meet WCAG contrast?
blocks.context: WCAG level AA asks for a **contrast ratio** of at least **4.5 : 1** for normal text, and **3 : 1** for large text (about 18 point, or 14 point bold). Aaron checks three colour pairs with a contrast checker.
steps: Black text on white: 21 : 1 (the maximum). **Passes.**

Mid-grey text on white, 4.0 : 1, at 24 point: 24 point counts as large text, which only needs 3 : 1, so it **passes**. The same grey at 14 point (not bold) would **fail**, because normal text needs 4.5 : 1.
Yellow text on white: about 1.1 : 1. **Fails** at any size.
blocks.answer: Higher ratio = easier to read. Aim well above the minimum.

blocks.text: The Accessibility Checker cannot check everything. It does not know whether your alt text is **accurate**, whether your words are easy to understand, or whether your animations flash too much. You still need to check with your own eyes.

head: Not accessible
Accessible
rows: Colour plus a word or symbol
24 pt or more, plain font, high contrast
Every slide has its own title

blocks.title: Key points
items: Accessibility means everyone can use your presentation.
Add alt text to every meaningful image; mark decorative ones.
Never use colour alone to show meaning: about 1 in 12 men are colour blind.
Large, plain, high-contrast text; a unique title on every slide.
WCAG is the international standard: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust; contrast at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text.
Run Review > Check Accessibility, then check by eye too.

check.q: What is alt text?
o: Text that appears when you hover over a link
A written description of an image for screen readers
Text hidden in the speaker notes
check.why: Alt text describes an image so screen reader users know what it shows.

check.q: Where is the Accessibility Checker in PowerPoint?
check.why: Review > Check Accessibility lists errors, warnings and tips.

check.q: A quiz shows correct answers in green and wrong answers in red, with no other sign. Why is this a problem?
o: Green and red are not available in PowerPoint
It makes the file too big
Colour-blind users may not tell them apart
Screen readers cannot read slides with colour
check.why: Red-green colour blindness is the most common type. Add a tick or cross as well.

check.q: What is WCAG?
o: An international standard of accessibility guidelines
check.why: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, from the W3C, are the international standard for accessible digital content.

check.q: Which is the best alt text for a photo of Belfast City Hall?
o: Belfast City Hall, a large stone building with a green dome
An image that I found on the internet
check.why: Good alt text says briefly what the image shows.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **alt text** and why it should be added to images in a presentation.
practice.a: A short text description of an image (1) that is read out by a screen reader so blind / visually impaired users know what the image shows (1).

practice.q: WCAG says content should be **perceivable**. Describe **two** ways a presentation can meet this.
practice.a: Any two: alt text on images (1); captions on video (1); high contrast text, e.g. at least 4.5 : 1 (1); large font size (1); not using colour alone to show meaning (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways a presentation can be made easier to use for someone who is colour blind.
practice.a: Any two: do not use colour alone to show meaning / add symbols or labels (1); avoid red/green combinations (1); use high contrast (1); add data labels to charts (1).

pages.spec: Use speaker notes, rehearse timings and Presenter View, and apply good speaking skills to deliver a presentation
pages.summary: Speaker notes hold what you will say; Presenter View shows them only to you while the audience sees the slides. Rehearse with timings, then speak clearly to the audience, not to the screen.

diagram.title: How long will my presentation be?
diagram.caption: Change the number of slides and the seconds you spend on each. Most class presentations have a time limit, so check you fit it.

blocks.text: The best slides in the world will not save a presentation that is mumbled at the screen. Delivering well is a skill, and like any skill it gets better with practice.
Speaker notes

**[[Speaker notes]]** are what you plan to say for each slide. Type them in the **Notes pane** under the slide (click **Notes** on the status bar if you cannot see it). The audience never sees them. This is where the detail goes that you took **off** the slide when you followed the 6x6 guideline.

blocks.title: Worked example: slide text vs notes
blocks.context: Slide 5 of Tiernan's presentation on renewable energy in Northern Ireland.
steps: **On the slide:** Wind power • Wind farms on hills and at sea • Turbines turn generators • No fuel needed.
**In the notes:** 'Wind is one of Northern Ireland's main sources of renewable electricity. You might have seen wind farms on the hills across Tyrone and Antrim…'
The slide gives the audience the headline; the notes remind Tiernan of the detail to say.
blocks.answer: Short keywords on the slide, full explanation in the notes.

blocks.text: Write your notes as **prompts**, not a script to read word for word. Reading aloud from notes sounds flat and you lose eye contact. Use short phrases that remind you what to say next.
Presenter View

When your computer is connected to a projector or second screen, **[[Presenter View]]** shows the audience only the slide, while **your** screen shows the current slide, the **next** slide, your speaker notes and a timer. Turn it on with **Slide Show > Use Presenter View** (it usually starts automatically with two screens). To practise with only one screen, start the show and click the **…** menu at the bottom left, then **Show Presenter View**, or press **Alt + F5**.
Rehearsing

**Slide Show > Rehearse Timings** runs the show with a timer so you can practise out loud. At the end PowerPoint tells you the total time and asks whether to **keep the timings**. Keep them only if you want the slides to move on by themselves (like a kiosk); for a normal talk, choose **No** and just use the information.

Microsoft 365 also has **Rehearse with Coach** (Speaker Coach), which listens as you practise and gives feedback on things like pace, filler words such as *um* and *like*, and whether you are reading the slide text word for word.

blocks.title: Worked example: will it fit?
blocks.context: Saoirse has a 5-minute limit. She has 12 slides and her rehearsal shows she spends about 30 seconds on each.
steps: Total time = 12 × 30 = 360 seconds.
She is 1 minute over. 60 seconds ÷ 30 seconds per slide = 2 slides.
Options: cut or merge 2 slides, or spend about 25 seconds on each slide (12 × 25 = 300 seconds = 5 minutes).
blocks.answer: 6 minutes: she must cut about 2 slides or speed up to about 25 seconds per slide.

blocks.text: Speaking skills

head: Skill
What it means
rows: Look at the audience, not the screen or your notes. Glance down, then look up again.
Speak loudly and clearly enough for the back row; slow down (nerves make everyone speed up).
A short pause after a key point lets it sink in. Silence is better than 'um'.
Stand up straight, face the audience, do not stand in front of the projector.
Practise enough that the slides are reminders, not a script.
Leave time at the end. If you don't know an answer, say so honestly.
blocks.caption: Speaking skills

items: **F5**: start from the beginning. **Shift + F5**: start from the current slide.
**N**, **Space**, **→** or **Enter**: next. **P** or **←**: previous.
Type a **slide number** then press **Enter** to jump to that slide.
**B**: black screen (press again to return). **W**: white screen.
**Esc**: end the show.

blocks.text: Never just **read your slides aloud** to the audience. They can read faster than you can talk, so they get bored. The slides show the key points; *you* explain them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Speaker notes hold what you will say; the audience does not see them.
Presenter View shows you the notes, next slide and timer; the audience sees only the slide.
Rehearse Timings measures how long your talk takes.
Make eye contact, speak clearly, pause, and do not read the slides out.
Check your total time against the time limit.

check.q: Who can see the speaker notes during a slide show using Presenter View?
check.why: Presenter View shows notes only on the presenter's screen.

check.q: Which feature measures how long you spend on each slide while you practise?
check.why: Rehearse Timings records the time for each slide and the whole show.

check.q: A presentation has 15 slides and the speaker spends 40 seconds on each. How long is it?
check.why: 15 × 40 = 600 seconds = 10 minutes.

check.q: During a slide show, which key turns the screen black so the audience looks at you?
check.why: B gives a black screen; press it again to return. W gives a white screen.

check.q: Which is the best advice about speaker notes?
o: Copy every word from the slide into them
Write prompts that remind you what to say
Leave them empty so you sound natural
Put them on the slide so you can see them
check.why: Short prompts help without turning the talk into reading aloud.

practice.q: Explain how **Presenter View** helps a speaker.
practice.a: The speaker can see their notes / next slide / a timer (1) while the audience only sees the current slide on the projector (1).

practice.q: Give **three** pieces of advice to a pupil about to deliver a presentation to their class.
practice.a: Any three: make eye contact (1); speak clearly / loudly enough (1); do not read the slides out word for word (1); rehearse beforehand / check timing (1); use pauses / slow down (1); face the audience, not the screen (1).

pages.spec: Evaluate a presentation against success criteria, using peer feedback, and refine it to improve usability
pages.summary: Evaluating means judging how well your presentation met its success criteria, using evidence such as peer feedback. A good evaluation names strengths, admits weaknesses, and says exactly how to improve.

diagram.title: The improvement cycle
diagram.caption: Evaluating is not the end: it feeds into the next version. Click each stage.

items.label: Set success criteria
items.detail: Agree what a good presentation must do, before you start building.

items.label: Build and present
items.detail: Create the slides from your storyboard and deliver them.

items.label: Gather feedback
items.detail: Ask peers to judge each criterion and give two stars and a wish.

items.label: Evaluate
items.detail: Compare the evidence with each criterion: met, partly met or not met, and why.

items.label: Improve
items.detail: Make specific changes, then check them against the criteria again.

blocks.text: When you finish a presentation, the job is not quite done. You need to **evaluate** it: decide how good it actually was, using **evidence**, and work out how to make it better. This is the **Evaluate** E in CCEA's Using ICT, and it is a skill you will use in every GCSE coursework task.
Success criteria

**[[Success criteria]]** are the checklist of what a good presentation must do. They are usually agreed **before** you start, so you know what you are aiming for. Good criteria are specific and can be checked.

head: Vague (hard to check)
Specific (easy to check)
rows: No more than 6 bullet points on any slide
One theme used on every slide; text at least 24 pt
Every image is relevant, has alt text and is credited
Lasts 4 to 5 minutes and the speaker makes eye contact

blocks.title: Worked example: success criteria for a class task
blocks.context: Task: a 5-minute presentation to Year 8 about staying safe online.
steps: 1. Suits a Year 8 audience: simple language, relevant examples.
2. Follows the 6x6 guideline; text at least 24 pt with strong contrast.
3. Uses one consistent theme and transition.
4. Includes at least one chart or SmartArt diagram.
5. Every image has alt text and is credited on a Sources slide.
6. Delivered in 4 to 5 minutes with eye contact and without reading the slides.
blocks.answer: Six checkable criteria covering audience, design, content, accessibility, sources and delivery.

blocks.text: Peer feedback

**Peer assessment** means classmates judge your work against the success criteria. They notice things you cannot, because you already know what you meant. A popular method is **two stars and a wish**: two things that were done well, and one specific thing to improve.

head: Unhelpful feedback
Helpful feedback
rows: "The pie chart on slide 4 made the survey results really clear."
"Slides 2 and 3 had about 10 lines each; could some of it go in your notes?"
"You read from the screen a lot, so we couldn't see your face. Try looking at us more."
blocks.caption: Make feedback specific, kind and useful

blocks.text: When giving feedback, be **kind, specific and helpful**. Talk about the work, not the person. When receiving feedback, listen and say thanks: it is information to help you, not an attack.
Writing an evaluation
A good evaluation goes through the criteria one by one and, for each, says whether it was met and **gives evidence**. Then it says **what you would improve** and **how**.

blocks.title: Worked example: evaluating one criterion
blocks.context: Criterion 2: *Follows the 6x6 guideline; text at least 24 pt with strong contrast.*
steps: **Judgement:** partly met.
**Evidence:** most slides had 4 or 5 bullet points, but peer feedback said slide 3 had 9 lines and was hard to read from the back.
**Improvement:** split slide 3 into two slides, cut each point to keywords and move the detail into the speaker notes.
blocks.answer: Judgement + evidence + specific improvement: that is what earns marks.

blocks.text: Refining for usability

Evaluating leads to **refining**: improving the product in small steps so it works better for its users. Designers talk about **[[usability|Usability]]** (how easy something is to use) and **user experience** (how it feels to use it). For a presentation that means: can the audience read it, follow it and understand it? For a quiz or kiosk: can a visitor work out what to click without help?

blocks.title: Worked example: refining a kiosk quiz
blocks.context: Version 1 of Cara's Fermanagh quiz was tested by three Year 8 pupils at the school open day.
steps: **Evidence:** two of the three testers got stuck on the 'Try again' slide because there was no button back.
**Evidence:** one tester could not tell the answer buttons from the pictures.
**Refinement (version 2):** add a Back button to every 'Try again' slide; give all answer buttons the same colour, a border and a word label.
**Re-test:** the next three testers finished the quiz without help.
blocks.answer: Test with real users, refine, then test again: each version is more usable than the last.

blocks.text: "I think my presentation was really good and I wouldn't change anything" is **not** an evaluation. Every piece of work can be improved, and saying exactly how shows you understand the criteria.

items: Did it suit the **audience** and achieve its **purpose**?
Was the **design** readable and consistent?
Were images **legal, relevant and credited**?
Was it **accessible**?
Did all **links and buttons** work?
Was the **delivery** clear and within the time limit?

blocks.title: Key points
items: Success criteria are a checklist of what a good presentation must do.
Make criteria specific so they can be checked.
Peer assessment: classmates judge your work against the criteria (two stars and a wish).
Good feedback is kind, specific and helpful.
Refine in small steps to improve usability, then test again with real users.
An evaluation gives a judgement, evidence and a specific improvement for each criterion.

check.q: What are success criteria?
o: The marks your teacher gives at the end
A checklist of what a good piece of work must do
check.why: Success criteria set out what the work must achieve, usually agreed before you start.

check.q: Which success criterion is the easiest to check?
o: There is not too much text
Every slide uses text of at least 24 pt
check.why: A specific, measurable criterion can be checked with a clear yes or no.

check.q: Which is the most helpful piece of peer feedback?
o: Add alt text to the photo on slide 5.
I liked it but it was too long.
check.why: It is specific and tells the presenter exactly what to do.

check.q: Testers keep getting stuck on one slide of a kiosk quiz. Improving it so it is easier to use is called…
check.why: Refining means improving a product in steps so it is easier to use (better usability).

check.q: A good evaluation of each criterion includes…
o: A judgement, evidence and a specific improvement
A list of every slide's title
Only the things that went well
The teacher's mark for the work
check.why: Judge it, back it up with evidence, then say exactly how to improve.

practice.q: Explain why **peer feedback** is useful when evaluating a presentation.
practice.a: Classmates see the presentation as the audience does / notice problems the author misses (1), giving evidence and ideas for specific improvements (1).

practice.q: Peer feedback says: *"Slide 6 had lots of text and you read it out word for word."* Suggest **two** improvements.
practice.a: Any two: cut text to keywords / follow 6x6 (1); move detail into speaker notes (1); split into two slides (1); rehearse so the speaker explains rather than reads (1); use a chart/image instead of text (1).

glossary.def: A program that shows information as a series of slides, usually to support a speaker, e.g. Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides or Apple Keynote.
The people who will watch or use a presentation. Their age, knowledge and needs affect every design choice.
What a presentation is meant to achieve, e.g. to inform, persuade, entertain or advertise.
Designing a product around the needs of the people who will use it, found by asking or observing them.
The accepted rules for communicating with a particular audience, e.g. how formal the language is, a title slide and a sources slide. Also called communication protocols.
A plan of every slide made before building a presentation, showing layout, text, images and their sources, effects, links and notes.
The strip of tools across the top of the PowerPoint window, organised into tabs (Home, Insert, Design…) and groups.
A ready-made arrangement of placeholders for a slide, e.g. Title Slide, Title and Content, Comparison.
A dotted box on a slide layout that holds a title, text or other content, e.g. 'Click to add title'.
A slide design guideline: no more than about six bullet points per slide and about six words per bullet point.
The difference between the colour of text and its background. High contrast makes text easier to read.
The top slide in a hidden set of master layouts (View > Slide Master). Changes to it, such as a logo or font, appear on every slide.
The legal right of a creator to control how their work is copied and used. In the UK it is automatic and protected by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
Something a person creates with their mind, such as a photo, song, design, logo or invention, that they own. Protected by copyright, trade marks and patents.
Permission from the owner of a work setting out what others may and may not do with it, e.g. a Creative Commons licence.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images, audio or video, from a prompt. AI-generated images should be clearly labelled.
Using someone else's work or ideas and presenting them as your own.
Free licences that let creators allow others to use their work under set conditions, e.g. BY (credit the creator), NC (non-commercial).
Giving credit to the creator of a work you use: Title, Author, Source and Licence (TASL).
A PowerPoint feature that turns a list into a ready-designed diagram such as a process, cycle or hierarchy.
An effect that plays when moving from one slide to the next, e.g. Fade or Morph.
An effect applied to an object on a slide: entrance, emphasis, exit or motion path.
A presentation where the user chooses which slide to go to next by clicking links or buttons, e.g. a quiz or menu.
Clickable text or an object that jumps to another slide, a web page, a file or an email address (Insert > Link, Ctrl + K).
A ready-made shape, such as Home, Back or Next, that performs an action like going to a slide when clicked (Insert > Shapes).
A slide show setting (Browsed at a kiosk) where the show runs full screen, loops, and can only be moved on with links, buttons or timings.
Designing something so that everyone can use it, including people with a disability.
Software that reads aloud the text on a screen, including alt text, for people who are blind or partially sighted.
Alternative text: a short written description of an image or chart that a screen reader reads aloud.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the international standard for accessible digital content, from the W3C. Its four principles are Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
A PowerPoint tool (Review > Check Accessibility) that lists errors, warnings and tips, such as missing alt text or slide titles.
Notes for the presenter about what to say for each slide. The audience does not see them.
A slide show view where the presenter sees the current slide, next slide, notes and a timer while the audience sees only the slide.
A checklist of what a good piece of work must do, used to plan and evaluate it.
How easy a product is for its users to use. Refining a product based on testing improves its usability.
